# Offer Enhancers — Scarcity, Urgency & Bonuses

**Source:** *$100M Offers*, "Enhancing Your Offer" (lines ~1979–2379).
These are the **outside** variables that position the core offer in the prospect's mind — "often more
powerful than your core offer" (l.2021). You build the offer once (see `offer-creation-5-step.md`);
these enhancers shift the demand curve *without changing the offer itself*.

The governing frame is the **Delicate Dance of Desire**. Scarcity, Urgency, and Bonuses are three of
the five enhancers (Guarantees → `guarantee-taxonomy.md`; Names → `magic-naming.md`).

---

## Governing principle — The Delicate Dance of Desire (l.1983–2033)

All marketing influences the supply/demand curve. **Increase demand → sell more units. Decrease
supply → sell each unit for more.** The "perfect profit combination" is *lots of demand and very
little supply (or perceived supply)* (l.1987).

- **Desire comes from *not* getting what you want.** > "Desire is a contract you make with yourself to
  be unhappy until you get what you want." (Naval Ravikant, quoted l.1993). We only want what we don't
  have — so to raise demand you must **delay or under-satisfy** it: sell *fewer* units than you can.
- Demand is **fractal (80/20), not linear** — "one fifth of the prospects are willing to pay five
  times the price (or more)" (l.2001). Skimming the top of the pyramid leaves pent-up demand that
  compounds each cycle.
- **Hormozi Law:** > "The longer you delay the ask, the bigger the ask you can make." (l.2011) — "the
  longer the runway, the bigger the plane that can take off."
- **The rule:** keep supply (and satisfaction of desire) *under* the demand you generate. Satisfy zero
  → no money; satisfy *all* → you "kill your golden goose." Master the dance between the two. Want the
  *ravenous* prospect, not merely the aroused (l.2019).

The five enhancers and what each does (l.2023–2031):
1. **Scarcity** — decrease supply to raise prices (indirectly raises demand via perceived exclusiveness).
2. **Urgency** — increase demand by decreasing the prospect's *action threshold*.
3. **Bonuses** — increase demand and perceived exclusivity.
4. **Guarantees** — increase demand by reversing risk. *(→ `guarantee-taxonomy.md`)*
5. **Names** — re-stimulate demand and expand awareness. *(→ `magic-naming.md`)*

---

# 1 · SCARCITY — a function of *quantity* (l.2037–2149)

Scarcity limits *how many*. It "pulls on our psychological fear of loss to get us to take action"
(l.2083) — and **fear of loss is stronger than desire for gain** (l.2083). Premium prices come from
*implied demand*: people assume high demand → low supply → it must be expensive (l.2041).

## The three types of scarcity (l.2085–2091)
1. **Limited Supply of Seats/Slots** — in general or over X period of time.
2. **Limited Supply of Bonuses.**
3. **Never available again.**

## Delivery method A — Physical Products (l.2095–2105)
Limited releases of flavors, colors, designs, sizes, etc. *Pattern:* "This month, we are releasing
100 boxes of mint chocolate cookie flavored protein bars."
- **Always sell out.** Better to sell out consistently than over-order and fail to create scarcity.
- **Cadence:** repeat over time but not too often — **once a month** is the sweet spot.
- **Announce the sellout.** Telling everyone you sold out is part of what makes it work — it adds
  social proof and makes fence-sitters desire it more next time.
- *Prior-art anchor:* Chanel sends only 1–2 of each piece per store, so every item is the last or
  second-to-last in stock — lets them price far above market (l.2105).

## Delivery method B — Services: three caps (l.2107–2117)
Pick the one that fits your model; all create ethical scarcity while you still take clients steadily.

| Cap | Rule | Example wording |
|---|---|---|
| **1. Total Business Cap** | Only accept **X clients total** at this service level (on-going). Creates a waiting list; periodically raise capacity 10–20% then re-cap. Best for highest tiers. | "My agency only will service twenty-five customers total. Period." |
| **2. Growth Rate Cap** | Only accept **X new clients per week** (on-going). Bank on your real weekly capacity and simply tell prospects the openings left. | "We only accept 5 new clients per week and we already have the first 3 spots taken…" |
| **3. Cohort Cap** | Only accept **X clients per class/cohort** on whatever cadence you choose. Adds operational rhythm + legitimate scarcity. | "We take on 100 clients 4 times a year. We open the doors then close them." |

## Honest Scarcity — the most ethical (l.2129–2133)
The easiest scarcity strategy is **honesty**: define a number you're willing to take in a period, then
advertise your real progress toward it. "Letting people know that you are three-fourths of the way to
capacity this week will move people over the edge" (l.2133). Being 81% to capacity also *implies
social proof* — and **only you get to draw where the line is "full."**

## Scarcity Pro Tips
- **Limited access for higher-ticket services (l.2119–2121):** works especially well on one-off
  workshops, trainings, events, seminars, consulting. **Have fewer spots than you think you can sell**
  — so next time everyone remembers you sold out fast. A compounding strategy.
- **Lead-magnet scarcity (l.2123–2127):** cap a free download (e.g. "only 20 new people per week"),
  let it run out, and route the rest to a notify list. Turns a "neat free download" into something not
  everyone can access — and raises consumption when they do get it.
- **Extreme Scarcity (l.2141–2143):** "If you don't hate money, sell a very limited supply of 1-on-1
  access." Use any medium from the **Delivery Cube** (direct message, email, phone, voice memo, Zoom…).
  Cap it *tiny*, price it *very high*, then tell people. Limit delivery to a format you don't hate.
- **Once You're Out, You Can Never Come Back (l.2145–2147):** cap the service level *and* say leavers
  can never return — makes people think hard about leaving. **Works best with small groups**; loses
  teeth as groups get big.

## Decision rule — WHEN to use each scarcity type
- Sell a **physical/consumable product** → limited-release + always-sell-out + announce-the-sellout.
- Sell an **ongoing service** and want steady flow → pick one cap: capacity-limited top tier →
  **Total Business Cap**; steady weekly intake → **Growth Rate Cap**; you want operational cadence →
  **Cohort Cap**.
- **Uncomfortable manufacturing scarcity / want zero phoniness** → **Honest Scarcity** (advertise real
  % to capacity).
- **Higher-ticket upsell, event, or 1-on-1 access** → limited-access / extreme-scarcity, priced high,
  fewer spots than you can sell.
- **Free lead magnet** → weekly download cap + notify list.

# 2 · URGENCY — a function of *time* (l.2151–2215)

Urgency limits *when* people can sign up, not how many. "Deadlines. Drive. Decisions." (l.2153).
Often paired with scarcity but conceptually separate. Four ethical, repeatable types:

## 1) Cohort-Based Rolling Urgency (l.2161–2183)
Start clients on a regular cadence; the next kickoff date *is* the deadline. Bonus: gives you a
choreographed onboarding.
- *Base wording:* "If you sign up today, I can get you in with our next group that kicks off on Monday,
  otherwise you'll have to wait until our next kickoff date."
- *Juiced version:* mention a just-opened spot ("a client dropped out, I have an opening for Monday…").
- **The less frequently you kick off, the more powerful this is.** Even every-other-week confers the nudge.
- **Fear-of-lost-sales rebuttal (l.2175–2179):** unfounded — on a week-long launch, **50–60% of sales
  come in the last 4 hours of the last day**. The people who "miss out" were never going to buy.
- **If a cohort just started and someone wants in (l.2181–2183):** either (1) offer a speedy
  personalized onboarding as a "bonus" to get them in now, or (2) *(preferred)* frame the wait as an
  advantage — more time to review materials / consult family or team, plus an extended payment plan
  "only available because the start date is far out."

## 2) Rolling Seasonal Urgency (l.2185–2195)
Real sign-up-date countdowns on landing pages and in copy — **the dates must be real** or you lose
credibility. Re-wrap the *same* promotion with a new seasonal name to get a genuine start/finish.
- *Sequence pattern:* "New Year Promotion ends Jan 30!" → "Valentines Lovers Promo" → "Sexy By Spring
  Special" → "Fools in Love April Promo." Same promo, new wrapper, ~5 minutes of editing.
- **Pro Tip — Local Businesses (l.2195):** this is Hormozi's **#1 strategy for local businesses** —
  they must vary marketing more often; a new dated wrapper on the same core service beats "same old."

## 3) Pricing or Bonus-Based Urgency (l.2197–2203)
Make the *promotion / price / bonus* the thing they could miss — lets year-round sellers use urgency
honestly. (Lying that you "won't service them after the date" is dishonest; the *deal* expiring is not.)
- *Wording:* "Let's get you started today so you can take advantage of the discount… I'm not sure how
  long we'll run it as we change them every 4 weeks."
- Interchangeable levers: pricing promo, discount, or added bonuses (free install, free onboarding, an
  extra workshop valued at $X) that you swap around the core offer.
- **Pro Tip — Clean Your Pipeline With Every Price Change (l.2203):** raising prices? Tell the pipeline
  "the price is going up, get in now." Shows strength and pulls in fence-sitters. **Never raise prices
  silently.**

## 4) Exploding Opportunity (l.2205–2211)
Sometimes you expose the prospect to an **arbitrage / market-inefficiency opportunity** that itself
decays with time — every second of delay costs disproportionate gains.
- *Examples:* eBay→Amazon arbitrage correcting over time; crypto/stock timing; getting on a new ad
  platform before competitors; "exploding" job offers where pay drops each day of delay.
- If you're in front of a genuinely decaying opportunity, **emphasize the decay.**

## Decision rule — WHEN to use each urgency type
- You **onboard in batches** → Cohort-Based Rolling Urgency (default; also best operationally).
- You run **digital launches / promotions** → Rolling Seasonal Urgency (real countdowns + seasonal wrappers).
- You **sell year-round and can't cap intake** → Pricing/Bonus-Based Urgency (expire the *deal*, not the service).
- The prospect faces a **genuinely time-decaying opportunity** → Exploding Opportunity.
- **Local business** → lead with Rolling Seasonal Urgency (the #1 local play), varied frequently.

# 3 · BONUSES — expand the price-to-value discrepancy (l.2223–2379)

Core principle (l.2231): **"A single offer is less valuable than the same offer broken into its
component parts and stacked as bonuses."** You raise the price-to-value gap by *increasing value*, not
cutting price — anchor the price to the core offer, then pile bonuses until the gap is "too big to
bear" (the "but wait… there's more!" infomercial logic).

- **Pro Tip — add bonuses instead of discounting (l.2239–2241):** never discount the core offer;
  discounting teaches customers your prices are negotiable. Adding value is a position of strength.

## Presenting bonuses — 1-on-1 vs group (l.2243–2251)
- **1-on-1:** **ask for the sale *first*, before offering bonuses.** If **yes** → *after* they sign,
  reveal the additional bonuses (creates a *wow experience*, reinforces the decision). If **no** →
  present a bonus that **matches their perceived obstacle**, then ask again; agree, add the bonus, ask
  if that's "fair enough." Reciprocity makes stacked bonuses hard to reject.
- (Group selling is out of scope of the book.)

## The Bonus Bullets — how to present each bonus (l.2253–2295) — capture ALL 11
1. **Always offer them** (use the bulleted bundle from Trim & Stack).
2. **Give it a special name with a benefit in the title.**
3. **Tell them:** (a) how it relates to their issue; (b) what it is; (c) how you discovered it / what
   you had to do to create it; (d) how it will specifically improve their life — i.e. make it
   **faster, easier, or less effort/sacrifice** (the Value Equation).
4. **Provide proof** it's valuable — a stat, a past client, or personal experience.
5. **Paint a vivid mental image** of their life *assuming they've already used it* and are enjoying the benefits.
6. **Always ascribe a price tag and justify it.**
7. **Tools & checklists beat additional trainings** — lower effort & time to consume → higher value
   (the Value Equation still reigns).
8. **Each bonus addresses a specific concern/obstacle** in the prospect's mind about why they can't or
   won't succeed (the bonus proves that belief incorrect).
9. **Solve their *next* problem** — what they'd logically realize they need next, before they hit it.
10. **The value of the bonuses should *eclipse* the value of the core offer** — widening the
    price-to-value gap and implying the core must be even more valuable.
11. **Add scarcity and urgency to the bonuses themselves** — puts the technique "on steroids."

## Bonuses with scarcity / urgency (l.2297–2307)
- **Scarcity v1:** "Only people who sign up for [program] get Bonus #1, 2, 3 — never for sale or
  available anywhere else." **Scarcity v2:** "I have 3 tickets left to my $5,000 virtual event; buy
  this program and get one of the last 3 as a bonus." *(Not time-bound — about exclusivity of access.)*
- **Urgency v1:** "If you buy **today**, I'll add [bonus] that normally costs $1,000, free — to reward
  action takers." *(Time-bound — miss today, lose the bonus.)*

## Advanced — Other People's Products & Services (l.2309–2355)
Get non-competing businesses to give their products/services as *your* bonuses in exchange for free
exposure to your customers (free marketing for them; high-value bonuses at no cost to you). Enough of
these can justify your entire price in savings alone.
- *Pain-clinic pattern:* a chiropractor gives 2 free adjustments ($100 value); a low-inflammation food
  company gives discounts ($50 savings); braces/orthotics discounts ($150); a health club gives a free
  PT session + a month of pool access ($100); pharmacy discounts ($100/mo) — repeat across many
  providers (ten chiropractors → ten free adjustments). A $400 offer's free bonuses can exceed $400.
- **Jedi move:** negotiate a **group discount *and* a commission to yourself.** *(Prestige Labs
  pattern: sponsored-athlete clients get 30% off; the athlete is paid 40% of net sales — everyone
  wins.)* Each bonus can become an indirect revenue stream (referral commissions) on customers you
  already paid to acquire.

## What should be a bonus vs. core offer (when you fulfill it) (l.2373–2375)
**Short answer: the Wow Factor** — something you wouldn't want someone to miss. Pull out the most
*distinct* pieces that can almost stand on their own and highlight them — especially things **short in
length but high in value** (checklists, infographics, a product-launch map). People won't pay a lot for
a standalone map, but as a *bonus* it's perceived as very valuable.

## Bonus sourcing habits (Summary, l.2361–2371)
1. **Create** checklists, tools, swipe files, scripts, templates — anything costly to make once but
   easy to give endlessly.
2. **Record** every workshop, webinar, event, and interview → reuse as bonuses to crush obstacles.
3. **Proactively negotiate** group discounts + referral commissions with adjacent businesses that solve
   the customer's *next* need.

## Decision rule — WHEN / how to deploy bonuses
- **Closing a deal** → add a bonus, never discount the core offer.
- **1-on-1 sale** → ask first; reveal bonuses after "yes," or add an obstacle-matched bonus after "no."
- **A specific objection is blocking the sale** → deploy the bonus whose benefit *reverses that exact
  obstacle* (Bullet 8).
- **Low fulfillment cost / want to justify the whole price for free** → stack Other People's Products
  & Services.
- **A distinct, short, high-value nugget is buried in your core** → pull it out and name it as a bonus
  (Wow Factor).

---

## Output contract for `hormozi-offer-enhancers`

Given a built Grand Slam Offer, produce, for *this* product:
1. **Scarcity plan** — which type(s) (physical limited-release / a named service cap / honest % to
   capacity / extreme 1-on-1 / lead-magnet cap), the specific numeric limit *the user sets* (never
   fabricated), and the sell-out/announce mechanic.
2. **Urgency plan** — which of the 4 types, the real deadline/cadence, and the exact wording lines.
3. **Bonus stack** — each bonus written through all 11 Bonus Bullets (named w/ benefit, relates-to-issue,
   what/how-discovered, faster/easier/less-effort payoff, proof, vivid image, **$ value the user fills
   or derives**, obstacle it reverses); note which use bonus-scarcity vs bonus-urgency; list any Other
   People's Products to pursue.
4. Every limit, deadline, and $ value is user-set/derived or a `<placeholder>` — **no fabricated numbers.**

## Sources and basis

*$100M Offers* — Delicate Dance of Desire (l.1983–2033); Scarcity: implied demand + creating scarcity
(l.2041–2083), three types (l.2085–2091), Physical Products (l.2095–2105), Services caps (l.2107–2117),
Honest Scarcity (l.2129–2133), Pro Tips: limited access / lead magnet / extreme / never-come-back
(l.2119–2147); Urgency: four types (l.2159–2211), fear-of-lost-sales math (l.2175–2179), Local Pro Tip
(l.2195), Clean-Your-Pipeline (l.2203); Bonuses: core principle (l.2231–2237), no-discount Pro Tip
(l.2239–2241), 1-on-1 vs group (l.2243–2251), Bonus Bullets (l.2253–2295), bonus scarcity/urgency
(l.2297–2307), Other People's Products (l.2309–2355), summary + bonus-vs-core (l.2361–2375).
